about.title: Foster City Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Foster City's mix of shopping centers, waterfront paths, and residential complexes near E Hillsdale Boulevard and SR-92 sees plenty of foot traffic year-round, and uneven pavement, wet floors, or poor lighting can turn an ordinary errand into an injury. California law puts the burden on the injured person to show the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn people about it. That's why what happens right after a fall matters so much: photos of the spot, names of witnesses, and a request to preserve any surveillance footage can make or break a claim later. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves; we're a free service that connects Foster City residents hurt in a fall with an independent attorney who can evaluate the property owner's responsibility, gather the evidence needed, and handle communications with insurers while you focus on recovering.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Foster City Fall

items.title: Notice Has to Be Proven
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney knows how to dig up maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records to establish that notice.

items.title: Surveillance Footage Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many businesses in Foster City overwrite security video within days or weeks. A quick preservation letter from an attorney can stop that footage from being erased.

items.title: Your Own Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, even if you were partly distracted or not watching your step, you may still recover a share of damages reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Foster City?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the fall happened on public property, such as a city sidewalk or a facility owned by a government entity, the deadline to act is much shorter, so it's worth having a claim reviewed quickly.

items.question: What if I fell at a shopping center along E Hillsdale Boulevard or Foster City Boulevard?
items.answer: Commercial properties along these corridors are expected to keep walkways reasonably safe and to address known hazards promptly. An attorney can help figure out who's responsible, whether that's the store, the property management company, or a maintenance contractor, and whether there's a pattern of prior incidents.

items.question: Do I need proof the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, California law generally requires showing the owner had actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition. This can include evidence like how long a spill or hazard existed, prior complaints, or an inspection history, which is why documenting the scene right after a fall is so valuable.
